questiontext.text: In usage-model statistical testing, a usage model is best described as:

answer.text: A Markov chain whose states are usage situations and whose transitions carry operational probabilities

feedback.text: Correct — the model is a Markov chain of states linked by probability-weighted transitions.

answer.text: A ranked list of test cases ordered by priority

feedback.text: No — a usage model is a state-transition chain, not a prioritised test list.

answer.text: A checklist of every screen the application contains

feedback.text: No — it captures how users move between situations with probabilities, not a screen inventory.

answer.text: A graph of response time versus concurrent load

feedback.text: That is a performance profile, unrelated to a usage model.

generalfeedback.text: A usage model is a Markov chain: states are usage situations (Home, Browse, Cart, Checkout, Exit) and each transition carries an operational probability. Tests are random walks weighted by that profile.

questiontext.text: Because the usage model is a Markov chain, the probability of the next transition depends on:

answer.text: Only the current state, not the earlier history of the walk

feedback.text: Correct — that memoryless property is exactly what makes it a Markov chain.

answer.text: The entire sequence of states already visited

feedback.text: No — a Markov chain is memoryless; only the current state matters.

answer.text: The total number of tests generated so far

feedback.text: No — each walk is independent and depends only on the current state.

answer.text: The wall-clock time already spent in the session

feedback.text: No — the chain has no notion of elapsed time; only the current state governs the next step.

generalfeedback.text: In a Markov chain the next transition is chosen using only the outgoing probabilities of the current state — the path taken to get there is irrelevant.

questiontext.text: The operational profile captured by the model is:

answer.text: The probabilities with which real users take each action — the distribution of actual usage

feedback.text: Correct — the operational profile is the real-usage distribution encoded on the transitions.

answer.text: The CPU and memory usage of the server

feedback.text: No — that is a resource profile, not the operational (usage) profile.

answer.text: A ranked list of the most severe defects

feedback.text: No — the operational profile describes user behaviour, not defect severity.

answer.text: The percentage of source code the suite covers

feedback.text: No — that is code coverage, not the operational profile.

generalfeedback.text: The operational profile is the probability distribution of how real users behave. Here it lives in the Prob. column: the likelihood a user in each state takes each outgoing action.

questiontext.text: A transition's probability (the Prob. column) represents:

answer.text: How likely a user in that state is to take that particular action next

feedback.text: Correct — it is the conditional probability of that action given the current state.

answer.text: How long that transition takes to execute

feedback.text: No — the probability is a likelihood, not a duration.

answer.text: How many defects that transition contains

feedback.text: No — the number is a usage likelihood, not a bug count.

answer.text: The cost of testing that transition

feedback.text: No — it measures how often users take the action, not testing cost.

generalfeedback.text: Each transition probability is the chance that a user currently in the "from" state takes that action next. The outgoing probabilities of a state form a distribution and sum to 1.

questiontext.text: In this explorer, a single generated test case corresponds to:

answer.text: One probability-weighted random walk from Home to Exit

feedback.text: Correct — each test is one random walk through the chain from the initial to the terminal state.

answer.text: One full enumeration of every path in the model

feedback.text: No — statistical testing samples walks; it does not enumerate all paths.

answer.text: A single transition chosen from the table

feedback.text: No — a test is a whole walk from Home to Exit, not one edge.

answer.text: One row of the coverage tally

feedback.text: No — the coverage tally counts walks; it is not itself a test.

generalfeedback.text: A generated test is one random walk that starts at Home and follows probability-weighted transitions until it reaches the absorbing Exit state.

questiontext.text: Statistical (usage-based) testing generates its tests by:

answer.text: Sampling walks at random, weighted by the operational profile, so common paths are tested more often

feedback.text: Correct — sampling by the usage distribution is the defining idea of statistical testing.

answer.text: Exhaustively covering every transition exactly once

feedback.text: No — that is a coverage criterion, not usage-weighted sampling.

answer.text: Always choosing the shortest path to Exit

feedback.text: No — walks are random and weighted by usage, not minimised.

answer.text: Always exercising the rarest transitions first

feedback.text: No — rare transitions are under-sampled precisely because sampling follows usage.

generalfeedback.text: Statistical testing draws random walks weighted by the operational profile. Effort therefore tracks real usage: frequently taken paths are exercised often, rare ones seldom.

questiontext.text: In the model, what is the probability that a user at Home goes to Browse?

feedback.text: Correct — the Home to Browse (browse) transition is 0.80.
No — 0.20 is the Home to Exit (leave) probability.
No — 0.50 appears on Browse and Cart transitions, not Home to Browse.
No — Home splits between Browse (0.80) and Exit (0.20).

generalfeedback.text: The table lists Home to Browse (browse) at p = 0.80; the only other outgoing edge, Home to Exit (leave), is 0.20.

questiontext.text: What is the probability that a user leaves directly from Home to Exit (the leave event)?

feedback.text: Correct — Home to Exit (leave) is 0.20.
No — 0.80 is the Home to Browse probability.
No — 0.10 is Cart to Exit (abandon), not Home to Exit.
No — Home's edges are 0.80 and 0.20.

generalfeedback.text: Home has two outgoing edges: browse (0.80) and leave to Exit (0.20). They sum to 1.

questiontext.text: What is the probability that a user in Cart proceeds to Checkout?

feedback.text: Correct — Cart to Checkout (checkout) is 0.50.
No — 0.40 is Cart to Browse (keepShopping).
No — 0.10 is Cart to Exit (abandon).
No — 1.00 is Checkout to Exit (pay), not Cart to Checkout.

generalfeedback.text: Cart splits three ways: keepShopping to Browse (0.40), checkout to Checkout (0.50), abandon to Exit (0.10). The checkout edge is 0.50.

questiontext.text: What is the probability of the pay transition, Checkout to Exit?

feedback.text: Correct — Checkout has one outgoing edge, pay to Exit, at 1.00.
No — 0.50 is Cart to Checkout, not Checkout to Exit.
No — Checkout always proceeds to Exit; its edge is 1.00.
No — 0.10 is Cart to Exit (abandon).

generalfeedback.text: Checkout has a single outgoing transition, pay to Exit, with probability 1.00, so its outgoing probabilities trivially sum to 1.

questiontext.text: Every generated walk begins in which state?

answer.text: Home

feedback.text: Correct — Home is the initial state of the model.

answer.text: Exit

feedback.text: No — Exit is the terminal state where walks end, not begin.

answer.text: Browse

feedback.text: No — Browse is reached from Home, it is not the start.

answer.text: Cart

feedback.text: No — Cart is an interior state, not the initial one.

generalfeedback.text: The model's initial state is Home; walks start there and end at the absorbing Exit state.

questiontext.text: Which state is the terminal (absorbing) state where every walk ends?

answer.text: Exit

feedback.text: Correct — Exit is absorbing: it has no outgoing transitions.

answer.text: Home

feedback.text: No — Home is the initial state, not the terminal one.

answer.text: Checkout

feedback.text: No — Checkout still has an outgoing pay transition to Exit.

answer.text: Cart

feedback.text: No — Cart has three outgoing transitions, so it is not absorbing.

generalfeedback.text: Exit is the absorbing terminal state: once a walk reaches it there are no outgoing edges, so the walk stops.

questiontext.text: The model shades one transition as rare (p < 0.15). Which transition is it?

answer.text: Cart to Exit (abandon), p = 0.10

feedback.text: Correct — abandon at 0.10 is the only transition below the 0.15 threshold.

answer.text: Home to Exit (leave), p = 0.20

feedback.text: No — 0.20 is above the 0.15 rare threshold.

answer.text: Browse to Exit (leave), p = 0.20

feedback.text: No — 0.20 is above the 0.15 rare threshold.

answer.text: Cart to Browse (keepShopping), p = 0.40

feedback.text: No — 0.40 is well above the rare threshold.

generalfeedback.text: The rare threshold is p < 0.15. Only Cart to Exit (abandon, 0.10) falls below it, so it is the single row flagged with the warning marker.

questiontext.text: What is the probability that a user in Browse views more (the self-loop Browse to Browse)?

feedback.text: Correct — the viewMore self-loop on Browse is 0.50.
No — 0.30 is Browse to Cart (addToCart).
No — 0.20 is Browse to Exit (leave).
No — 0.80 is the Home to Browse probability, not the Browse self-loop.

generalfeedback.text: Browse has three outgoing edges: viewMore back to Browse (0.50), addToCart to Cart (0.30), leave to Exit (0.20). The self-loop is 0.50.

questiontext.text: The explorer reports the expected test-case length for this model as about:

answer.text: 4.05 transitions

feedback.text: Correct — the app displays an expected length of 4.05 transitions for this chain.

answer.text: 5 transitions (one per state)

feedback.text: No — expected length is not simply the number of states; loops and probabilities change it.

answer.text: 9 transitions (one per edge)

feedback.text: No — it is not the number of edges in the table.

answer.text: 1.00 transition

feedback.text: No — most walks take several transitions before reaching Exit.

generalfeedback.text: The absorbing-chain expected number of steps from Home is about 4.05 transitions, which the explorer shows beneath the model table.

questiontext.text: Why must the outgoing probabilities of every state sum to exactly 1?

answer.text: They form a probability distribution over the user's next action — the user takes exactly one outgoing transition

feedback.text: Correct — the edges out of a state are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so they sum to 1.

answer.text: Because every state has the same number of outgoing transitions

feedback.text: No — states have different numbers of edges (Checkout has one, Cart three); the sum is 1 regardless.

answer.text: So the expected test length comes out to a whole number

feedback.text: No — the expected length is 4.05, not a whole number; that is unrelated to the sum being 1.

answer.text: To guarantee every transition is exercised at least once

feedback.text: No — summing to 1 does not guarantee coverage; rare edges are often missed.

generalfeedback.text: From any state a user must take exactly one of the available actions next. The outgoing edges are therefore a probability distribution and must sum to 1 (Home: 0.8+0.2; Browse: 0.5+0.3+0.2; Cart: 0.4+0.5+0.1).

questiontext.text: Browse has viewMore = 0.50, addToCart = 0.30 and leave = 0.20. Their sum is:

answer.text: 1.00 — a valid probability distribution

feedback.text: No — that omits one edge; the three sum to 1.00.
No — 0.50 is only the self-loop; all three edges together sum to 1.00.

generalfeedback.text: 0.50 + 0.30 + 0.20 = 1.00. Every state's outgoing probabilities must sum to 1, which the model note states explicitly.

questiontext.text: Because walks are weighted by the operational profile, testing effort is concentrated on:

answer.text: The paths real users take most often

feedback.text: Correct — usage weighting steers effort onto the common paths.

answer.text: The paths that are hardest to reach

feedback.text: No — hard-to-reach (rare) paths are under-sampled, not favoured.

answer.text: Every path equally, regardless of usage

feedback.text: No — that would be uniform sampling, not usage weighting.

answer.text: Only the single shortest path to Exit

feedback.text: No — walks are random; many different-length paths are generated.

generalfeedback.text: Sampling by the operational profile means high-probability paths are walked most often, so testing effort tracks real usage and reliability reflects the field experience.

name.text: Path probability: Home to Browse to Exit

questiontext.text: What is the probability of the exact walk Home → Browse → Exit (browse then leave)?

feedback.text: No — that is only the Browse to Exit edge; multiply by 0.80 for the whole walk.
No — path probability is the product of the edges, not their sum halved.
No — this is one specific walk among many; its probability is 0.16.

generalfeedback.text: Multiply the edge probabilities along the walk: Home to Browse (0.80) × Browse to Exit (0.20) = 0.16.

questiontext.text: What is the probability of the successful-purchase walk Home → Browse → Cart → Checkout → Exit?

feedback.text: No — that is only 0.80 × 0.30; continue multiplying by 0.50 and 1.00.
No — 0.06 is a longer walk with one extra viewMore loop, not this direct one.
No — that mis-multiplies the edges; the product is 0.12.

generalfeedback.text: 0.80 (browse) × 0.30 (addToCart) × 0.50 (checkout) × 1.00 (pay) = 0.12. This is the shortest successful-purchase path.

questiontext.text: A user in Cart is most likely to:

answer.text: Proceed to Checkout (p = 0.50)

feedback.text: Correct — checkout at 0.50 is the largest of Cart's outgoing probabilities.

answer.text: Keep shopping, returning to Browse (p = 0.40)

feedback.text: No — 0.40 is second; checkout at 0.50 is more likely.

answer.text: Abandon to Exit (p = 0.10)

feedback.text: No — abandon at 0.10 is the least likely action.

answer.text: Return directly to Home

feedback.text: No — there is no Cart to Home transition in the model.

generalfeedback.text: Cart's edges are keepShopping (0.40), checkout (0.50) and abandon (0.10). The largest is checkout at 0.50, so proceeding to Checkout is the most likely next action.

questiontext.text: Within this model, the operational profile is played by which element?

answer.text: The set of transition probabilities on the edges

feedback.text: Correct — the probabilities on the transitions are the operational profile.

answer.text: The list of states (Home, Browse, Cart, Checkout, Exit)

feedback.text: No — the states are the situations; the profile is the probabilities weighting the moves between them.

answer.text: The buggy-transition marker on Cart to Checkout

feedback.text: No — the bug marker flags a fault; it is not the usage distribution.

answer.text: The expected-length number shown below the table

feedback.text: No — the expected length is derived from the profile, it is not the profile itself.

generalfeedback.text: The operational profile is the probability distribution over user actions, i.e. the numbers in the Prob. column on the transitions. States and derived numbers are not the profile.

questiontext.text: Once a walk reaches Checkout, how many further transitions until Exit (expected)?

answer.text: Exactly 1 — Checkout to Exit (pay) has probability 1.0

feedback.text: Correct — Checkout has a single edge to Exit, so exactly one more step is taken.

answer.text: 0 — Checkout is already the terminal state

feedback.text: No — the terminal state is Exit; Checkout still takes one pay step to reach it.

answer.text: 2 — pay then a confirmation

feedback.text: No — the model has only the single pay transition out of Checkout.

answer.text: It varies randomly between 0 and 3

feedback.text: No — with a single probability-1.0 edge, it is deterministically one step.

generalfeedback.text: Checkout's only outgoing edge is pay to Exit with probability 1.0, so E[Checkout] = 1: exactly one more transition.

questiontext.text: Exit is called an absorbing state because:

answer.text: It has no outgoing transitions, so once a walk enters Exit it stops

feedback.text: Correct — no edges leave Exit, so the walk terminates there.

answer.text: It has the highest outgoing probability

feedback.text: No — Exit has no outgoing edges at all.

answer.text: It loops back to Home to restart the session

feedback.text: No — there is no Exit to Home edge; the walk ends.

answer.text: It is where the injected bug lives

feedback.text: No — the bug is on Cart to Checkout, not on Exit.

generalfeedback.text: An absorbing state has no outgoing transitions. Every walk that reaches Exit ends there, which is why the expected length is finite and well defined.

name.text: Which transition makes a test fail

questiontext.text: In this explorer a generated test "fails" when its walk fires which transition?

answer.text: Cart to Checkout — the checkout event, marked with a bug icon

feedback.text: Correct — the injected fault sits on Cart to Checkout, so any walk that fires it fails.

answer.text: Checkout to Exit (pay)

feedback.text: No — pay is not the buggy edge; the bug is on Cart to Checkout.

answer.text: Cart to Exit (abandon)

feedback.text: No — abandon is the rare edge, not the buggy one.

answer.text: Home to Browse (browse)

feedback.text: No — this common edge is not where the fault lives.

generalfeedback.text: The model plants the bug on the Cart to Checkout transition. A test fails if and only if its random walk fires that transition; otherwise it passes.

questiontext.text: What is the probability of the walk Home → Browse → Cart → Exit (abandon)?

feedback.text: No — that is only the Cart to Exit edge; multiply by the earlier edges too.
No — that is 0.80 × 0.30 (reaching Cart); still multiply by 0.10 for abandon.
No — the product is 0.024, not 0.048.

generalfeedback.text: 0.80 (browse) × 0.30 (addToCart) × 0.10 (abandon) = 0.024. The rare abandon edge makes this walk unlikely.

name.text: Why weight by usage rather than uniformly

questiontext.text: Compared with testing every path equally, weighting tests by the operational profile yields a reliability estimate that:

answer.text: Reflects the failures users are actually likely to experience in the field

feedback.text: Correct — usage weighting makes the estimate a field-relevant reliability.

answer.text: Guarantees 100% path coverage of the model

feedback.text: No — sampling by usage does not guarantee coverage; rare paths are often missed.

answer.text: Is always higher than the true reliability

feedback.text: No — the estimate is unbiased for usage-weighted reliability, not systematically higher.

answer.text: Ignores the most common paths entirely

feedback.text: No — it emphasises common paths, the opposite of ignoring them.

generalfeedback.text: Usage-weighted reliability answers "how often will a real user hit a failure?" Because tests are sampled from the operational profile, the pass rate estimates the reliability users actually experience.

questiontext.text: The rare-path warning flags abandon (Cart to Exit, p = 0.10) because statistical testing will:

answer.text: Rarely generate walks that traverse it, so it is under-sampled

feedback.text: Correct — low usage probability means few walks ever fire that edge.

answer.text: Test it more than any other transition

feedback.text: No — low probability means it is exercised least, not most.

answer.text: Never be able to reach Cart at all

feedback.text: No — Cart is reachable (p = 0.48); it is the abandon edge specifically that is rare.

answer.text: Automatically treat it as the highest-risk path

feedback.text: No — usage weighting does not know risk; that is why risk-based testing is suggested as a supplement.

generalfeedback.text: Because sampling follows usage, a low-probability edge like abandon (0.10) is walked seldom and thus under-tested. If such a rare path were also high-risk, usage weighting alone would leave it dangerously under-exercised.

name.text: Probability of reaching Cart in two steps

questiontext.text: What is the probability that a session's first two transitions are Home → Browse → Cart (reaching Cart in exactly two steps)?

feedback.text: No — that is only the Browse to Cart edge; multiply by the Home to Browse edge too.
No — the product of 0.80 and 0.30 is 0.24, not 0.11.

generalfeedback.text: Home to Browse (0.80) × Browse to Cart (0.30) = 0.24. Note this is only the two-step path; Cart can also be reached via the Browse self-loop, so total reachability is higher.

questiontext.text: In the transition-coverage tally shown after a run, each bar counts:

answer.text: How many of the generated random walks traversed that transition

feedback.text: Correct — the tally counts how often each edge was fired across all tests.

answer.text: The probability written on that transition

feedback.text: No — the probability is fixed in the model; the tally counts actual traversals.

answer.text: The number of states between that edge and Exit

feedback.text: No — it is a traversal count, not a distance.

answer.text: The expected test length contributed by that edge

feedback.text: No — the bars are observed counts from the run, not expected-length contributions.

generalfeedback.text: Each coverage bar is the observed number of generated walks that fired that transition. High-usage edges get tall bars; the rare abandon edge gets the shortest.

questiontext.text: Using E[s] = 1 + Σ p(s→s′)·E[s′] over the transient states, the expected length of a generated test (starting at Home) is closest to:

answer.text: 4.05 transitions

feedback.text: Correct — solving the recurrence gives E[Home] ≈ 4.05.

answer.text: 3.05 transitions

feedback.text: No — that undercounts; E[Home] = 1 + 0.8·E[Browse] ≈ 4.05.

answer.text: 5.00 transitions

feedback.text: No — the number of states is not the expected length.

answer.text: 9.00 transitions

feedback.text: No — the number of edges is not the expected length.

generalfeedback.text: E[Checkout] = 1; E[Cart] = 1 + 0.4·E[Browse] + 0.5·1; E[Browse] = 1 + 0.5·E[Browse] + 0.3·E[Cart] giving E[Browse] ≈ 3.82 and E[Cart] ≈ 3.03; then E[Home] = 1 + 0.8·3.82 ≈ 4.05.

questiontext.text: The expected number of remaining transitions to Exit starting from Cart is closest to:

feedback.text: No — 1.00 is E[Checkout]; Cart can loop back through Browse, making it larger.
No — 3.82 is E[Browse]; E[Cart] is a little smaller at 3.03.
No — 4.05 is E[Home], the full-walk expectation.

generalfeedback.text: E[Cart] = 1 + 0.4·E[Browse] + 0.5·E[Checkout] + 0.1·0 = 1.5 + 0.4·3.82 ≈ 3.03 (the 0.5·1 comes from the direct checkout-then-pay path).

questiontext.text: The expected number of remaining transitions to Exit starting from Browse is closest to:

feedback.text: Correct — solving 0.5·E[Browse] = 1 + 0.3·E[Cart] gives E[Browse] ≈ 3.82.
No — 2.00 ignores the Cart contribution; the self-loop and addToCart raise it to 3.82.
No — 3.03 is E[Cart]; E[Browse] is slightly larger.
No — 4.05 is E[Home].

generalfeedback.text: E[Browse] = 1 + 0.5·E[Browse] + 0.3·E[Cart], so 0.5·E[Browse] = 1 + 0.3·3.03, giving E[Browse] ≈ 3.82. The viewMore self-loop inflates it.

questiontext.text: Over a whole walk (including the Browse self-loop), what is the probability that a session reaches Cart at all?

feedback.text: Correct — 0.8 × 0.6 = 0.48, where 0.6 is the chance of eventually leaving Browse via addToCart.
No — 0.24 is only the two-step path; the Browse self-loop gives extra chances to reach Cart.
No — 0.30 is just the addToCart edge probability, ignoring reaching and looping in Browse.
No — 0.60 is the chance of reaching Cart given you are in Browse; multiply by 0.8 to reach Browse first.

generalfeedback.text: From Browse, P(reach Cart) = g where g = 0.5g + 0.3, so g = 0.6 (the self-loop keeps offering the 0.3 vs 0.2 choice). Reaching Browse first is 0.8, so P(reach Cart) = 0.8 × 0.6 = 0.48.

questiontext.text: What is the probability that a generated walk reaches Checkout (i.e. the session's conversion probability)?

feedback.text: Correct — the only way into Checkout is Cart to Checkout, whose overall probability is about 0.316.
No — 0.50 is the Cart to Checkout edge; you must also reach Cart, lowering the total to 0.316.
No — 0.48 is the probability of reaching Cart; only half of those go on to Checkout.
No — 0.12 is one specific purchase path; other paths (with loops) also reach Checkout, giving 0.316.

generalfeedback.text: P(reach Checkout) = P(reach Cart) × P(checkout | in Cart, eventually) . Solving f(Cart) = 0.5 + 0.4·f(Browse), f(Browse) = 0.6·f(Cart) gives f(Home) ≈ 0.316. This equals the fraction of sessions that fire the buggy edge.

questiontext.text: A test fails exactly when its walk fires Cart to Checkout. What is the model's true usage-weighted reliability (the probability a walk does not fire it)?

feedback.text: Correct — 1 − P(fire Cart to Checkout) = 1 − 0.316 ≈ 0.684.
No — 0.50 is the checkout edge probability alone, not the overall pass rate.
No — that overstates reliability; about 31.6% of walks fire the buggy edge.
No — 0.316 is the failure probability; reliability is its complement, 0.684.

generalfeedback.text: The probability of firing the buggy Cart to Checkout edge is about 0.316, so the usage-weighted reliability is 1 − 0.316 ≈ 0.684. A run's displayed estimate fluctuates around this value.

name.text: Path probability with one browse loop

questiontext.text: What is the probability of the walk Home → Browse → Browse → Cart → Checkout → Exit (one viewMore loop before adding to cart)?

feedback.text: No — 0.12 is the walk without the extra viewMore loop; the loop multiplies by 0.50.
No — the product is 0.06, not 0.03.
No — 0.024 is the abandon walk, a different path.

generalfeedback.text: 0.80 (browse) × 0.50 (viewMore) × 0.30 (addToCart) × 0.50 (checkout) × 1.00 (pay) = 0.06 — exactly half the loop-free purchase path (0.12), since the extra viewMore step costs a factor of 0.50.

name.text: Why expected length is not a plain count

questiontext.text: Why is the expected test length (4.05) not simply the number of states or edges in the model?

answer.text: The Browse self-loop lets walks revisit states, so length is a probability-weighted average that can exceed any single path's step count

feedback.text: Correct — loops and branching make length a weighted expectation, not a fixed count.

answer.text: Because the probabilities do not sum to 1, the count is scaled down

feedback.text: No — the probabilities do sum to 1; the reason is looping and branching, not scaling.

answer.text: Because every walk visits all five states exactly once

feedback.text: No — most walks skip states and some revisit Browse; visits are not uniform.

answer.text: Because the expected length ignores the terminal state

feedback.text: No — the recurrence accounts for reaching Exit; the driver is the looping structure.

generalfeedback.text: Different walks have different lengths, and the viewMore self-loop can extend a walk arbitrarily. The expected length is the probability-weighted average over all these walks (E[Home] ≈ 4.05), which is why it is not a simple state or edge count.

questiontext.text: The explorer reports a 95% interval of ±1.96·√(r(1−r)/n). If a run of n = 100 tests gives reliability r = 0.50, the half-width is closest to:

feedback.text: No — that omits the √(r(1−r)/n) factor; the half-width is 0.098.
No — 0.5% would need a far larger n; here it is 9.8%.
No — 0.25 is r(1−r), not the interval; you must divide by n and take the root.

name.text: How many tests to halve the interval

questiontext.text: The confidence interval scales as 1/√n. Going from the 50-test button to which count roughly halves the interval half-width?

answer.text: 200 tests (four times as many)

feedback.text: Correct — halving 1/√n needs 4× the sample, so 50 to 200.

answer.text: 100 tests (twice as many)

feedback.text: No — doubling n only shrinks the interval by 1/√2 ≈ 0.71, not to a half.

answer.text: 75 tests

feedback.text: No — that barely changes the interval; you need 4× the sample.

answer.text: 1000 tests

feedback.text: No — 1000 shrinks it by about 1/√20; to merely halve it, 200 suffices.

generalfeedback.text: Because the half-width is proportional to 1/√n, halving it requires quadrupling n. The explorer's 50 and 200 buttons differ by exactly 4×, so 200 tests give roughly half the interval of 50.

questiontext.text: Why does usage-weighted testing deliberately prioritise common paths over rare ones?

answer.text: Failures on common paths affect the most users, so testing them most heavily maximises delivered reliability

feedback.text: Correct — effort follows usage so the reliability estimate matches what users experience.

answer.text: Common paths are always the hardest to implement correctly

feedback.text: No — difficulty is unrelated; the rationale is user impact and field reliability.

answer.text: Rare paths can never contain defects

feedback.text: No — rare paths can be buggy; that is exactly the rare-but-risky gap the app warns about.

answer.text: It guarantees full path coverage of the model

feedback.text: No — it does not guarantee coverage; it targets usage-weighted reliability.

generalfeedback.text: A defect on a heavily used path fails many sessions, while one on a rarely used path fails few. Weighting tests by usage concentrates effort where failures hurt most, so the measured reliability reflects real user experience.

questiontext.text: The abandon edge (p = 0.10) is under-sampled. If that rare path were also safety-critical, the right response would be to:

answer.text: Supplement usage-based testing with risk-based testing to force coverage of the rare-but-risky path

feedback.text: Correct — usage weighting ignores risk, so add risk-based testing for high-risk rare paths.

answer.text: Rely on the statistical run alone, since it already covers everything

feedback.text: No — it under-samples rare edges, so a critical rare path may go untested.

answer.text: Delete the abandon transition from the model

feedback.text: No — the transition is a real behaviour; removing it would make the model wrong.

answer.text: Raise the abandon probability so it is sampled more

feedback.text: No — falsifying the operational profile would distort the reliability estimate.

generalfeedback.text: Usage weighting distributes effort by frequency, not by risk. A rare but high-risk path needs explicit risk-based testing on top of the statistical run — which is exactly why the explorer bridges to the risk-based testing view.

name.text: Which transition the tally exercises most

questiontext.text: After a large run, which transition will the coverage tally have exercised most heavily?

answer.text: Browse to Browse (viewMore) — the self-loop repeats and Browse is on the main path

feedback.text: Correct — the self-loop is fired about 1.05 times per walk on average, the highest of any edge.

answer.text: Cart to Exit (abandon)

feedback.text: No — abandon is the rarest edge (about 0.06 firings per walk), the least exercised.

answer.text: Checkout to Exit (pay)

feedback.text: No — pay is only reached in about 31.6% of walks, far less than the Browse self-loop.

answer.text: Cart to Checkout (checkout)

feedback.text: No — the buggy edge fires in about 31.6% of walks, well below the self-loop's average.

generalfeedback.text: Browse is visited about 2.1 times per walk and takes its self-loop with probability 0.5, so viewMore fires about 1.05 times per walk on average — more than any other edge. The abandon edge, at about 0.06 per walk, is exercised least.

questiontext.text: Suppose real users abandon far more than the model assumes (true Cart to Exit is much higher, Cart to Checkout lower). Compared with reality, the explorer's reliability estimate would be:

answer.text: Biased: because the model over-weights the buggy checkout edge, it under-estimates the reliability real users experience

feedback.text: Correct — a wrong profile biases the usage-weighted reliability; here the model fires the bug too often relative to reality.

answer.text: Unaffected, because reliability does not depend on the profile

feedback.text: No — usage-weighted reliability depends entirely on the transition probabilities.

answer.text: Exactly correct, because the chain is a Markov chain

feedback.text: No — being Markov does not make a wrong profile accurate; the numbers must match real usage.

answer.text: Always higher than reality regardless of which edges are wrong

feedback.text: No — the direction of bias depends on which way the probabilities are wrong.

generalfeedback.text: The reliability estimate is only as good as the operational profile. If the model over-weights the buggy Cart to Checkout edge relative to true abandonment, it fires the bug more often than real users would, biasing the estimate. A wrong profile can under- or over-state reliability and can leave the truly common bugs under-tested.

name.text: Why reliability equals one minus conversion

questiontext.text: In this model the usage-weighted reliability (≈0.684) is exactly 1 minus the conversion probability (≈0.316). Why do these two numbers coincide?

answer.text: The bug sits on Cart to Checkout, the only edge into Checkout, so a walk fails if and only if it converts

feedback.text: Correct — firing the buggy edge and reaching Checkout are the same event, so failure probability equals conversion.

answer.text: By coincidence; there is no structural reason

feedback.text: No — it is structural: the buggy edge is precisely the single entry into Checkout.

answer.text: Because the pay edge (Checkout to Exit) is also buggy

feedback.text: No — only Cart to Checkout is buggy; pay is not.

answer.text: Because every walk reaches Checkout eventually

feedback.text: No — only about 31.6% of walks reach Checkout; the rest exit earlier and pass.

generalfeedback.text: Cart to Checkout is both the only way into Checkout and the buggy edge, so "fires the bug", "reaches Checkout" and "converts" are the same event. Hence failure probability = conversion ≈ 0.316 and reliability = 1 − 0.316 ≈ 0.684.
